title: Cerebral Palsy, Developmental Neurology & Movement Disorders

76.from: Day 16 Q41 — Physiological versus fixed S2 splitting

84.from: Day 10 Q8 — CPS 72 h versus PES >48 h

added_station_answers.Station 1: Absent fidgety movements (cramped-synchronized repertoire) at about 3–5 months corrected age are among the strongest early predictors of CP. MRI adds the lesion site, the likely motor topography and aetiology; together with HINE this supports an early 'high risk of CP' diagnosis so that early intervention starts now rather than after a 'wait and see' period.
added_station_answers.Station 2: Periventricular white-matter injury (PVL) in an ex-28-week infant classically predicts bilateral spastic CP with legs more affected than arms (spastic diplegia), because the leg fibres run closest to the ventricles. Uncertainty: the MRI does not predict functional level (GMFCS) or exclude arm involvement; extensive lesions may give quadriplegia, and function must be followed clinically.
added_station_answers.Station 3: Reimers migration percentage = 6.8 ÷ 20 × 100 = 34%. A hip with MP above about 30% is 'at risk': refer to orthopaedics and shorten the surveillance interval; MP around 40% or more usually prompts consideration of preventive or reconstructive surgery. MP is interpreted with GMFCS level, age, pain, examination and the trend over time — not as a stand-alone operative indication.
added_station_answers.Station 4: A marked catch on fast stretch with nearly full range on slow stretch (a large Tardieu R1–R2 gap) indicates dynamic spasticity, not fixed contracture. This favours tone-reducing treatment (e.g. targeted botulinum toxin with stretching/orthoses) over tendon-lengthening surgery.
added_station_answers.Station 5: Chorea: brief, irregular, unpredictable, flowing movements that migrate between body parts. Dystonia gives sustained or intermittent patterned twisting postures; tics are stereotyped, preceded by an urge and briefly suppressible; tremor is a regular rhythmic oscillation.

added_why_not.Reassurance until school age: Clear hand preference before 12 months with abnormal tone and reflexes is a red flag; waiting loses the window for early intervention.
added_why_not.Electromyography as the first investigat: EMG assesses nerve and muscle (lower motor neuron) disease; upper motor neuron signs call for clinical neurological assessment and brain MRI first.
added_why_not.Diagnosis of simple handedness without e: True handedness is not established before about 18–24 months; a fisted thumb-in-palm and brisk reflexes on one side are pathological.
added_why_not.Definite spinal muscular atrophy based o: SMA is a lower motor neuron disease with hypotonia, weakness and areflexia, confirmed genetically; absent fidgety movements with a brain lesion point to CP.
added_why_not.Normal developmental variation requiring: Absent fidgety general movements are a strong predictor of CP, not a normal variant, especially with a supportive MRI lesion.
added_why_not.Wait for walking age before any disclosu: Current guidance recommends early 'high risk of CP' disclosure so family-centred intervention can start during peak neuroplasticity.
added_why_not.HINE score proves normal development: A HINE of 58 at 9 months is below the usual optimal cut-off (about 63–73 for this age), so it raises CP risk rather than proving normality.
added_why_not.HINE can only be used after age 5 years: The HINE is designed for infants aged roughly 2–24 months; it is one of the main early-detection tools.
added_why_not.A normal EEG excludes cerebral palsy: EEG assesses seizures and cortical function; CP is a clinical diagnosis supported by motor assessment and neuroimaging, not by EEG.
added_why_not.Accept regression as expected evolution: CP is non-progressive; loss of acquired skills is a red flag for a progressive neurometabolic, neurodegenerative or genetic disorder.
added_why_not.Diagnose spastic diplegia from regressio: Regression is not a feature of any CP subtype and cannot define the motor topography.
added_why_not.Focus exclusively on orthoses without ev: Orthoses manage function but do not address a possible progressive disease behind the regression; reassessment comes first.
added_why_not.Pure dystonia from basal ganglia injury: Dystonia follows deep grey-matter injury; leg-predominant spasticity with periventricular white-matter injury is spastic diplegia.
added_why_not.Flaccid paralysis from anterior horn cel: Anterior horn cell disease gives hypotonia and areflexia; hyperreflexia indicates an upper motor neuron lesion.
added_why_not.Isolated ataxia from cerebellar vermian: Vermian lesions cause truncal ataxia without hyperreflexia; periventricular white-matter injury causes spastic diplegia.
added_why_not.Dystonia rules out cerebral palsy: Dyskinetic (dystonic or choreoathetoid) CP is a recognised CP type, typically after basal ganglia–thalamic injury.
added_why_not.Isolated spastic diplegia is mandated by: Deep grey (basal ganglia–thalamic) injury causes dyskinetic CP; spastic diplegia relates to periventricular white-matter injury.
added_why_not.Congenital myopathy is proven by dystoni: Myopathies cause weakness and hypotonia, not dystonia; dystonia after encephalopathy with deep grey injury indicates dyskinetic CP.
added_why_not.GMFCS level V regardless of age: Level V means transported in a manual wheelchair with very limited head and trunk control; this child walks indoors with a hand-held device.
added_why_not.GMFCS level I: Level I children walk without limitation, including outdoors and on stairs, and run and jump.
added_why_not.GMFCS level II by definition of unaided: Level II children walk without a hand-held mobility device in most settings; needing a hand-held device indoors is level III.
added_why_not.GMFCS level II: Level II children walk in most settings without a hand-held device, which is not compatible with severely limited head and trunk control.
added_why_not.GMFCS level III with independent walking: Level III children walk indoors with a hand-held mobility device; severely limited head and trunk control with full transport assistance is level V.
added_why_not.CFCS level V: CFCS rates communication, not hand use; level V means communication is seldom effective even with familiar partners.
added_why_not.EDACS level V: EDACS rates eating and drinking safety; level V means unable to eat or drink safely. It does not classify handling objects.
added_why_not.Assign GMFCS level from conversational f: GMFCS classifies gross motor function and mobility only; it says nothing about communication.
added_why_not.Use MACS as a language impairment score: MACS classifies how a child handles objects in daily activities; communication is classified with CFCS.
added_why_not.Use hip migration percentage for languag: Reimers migration percentage measures lateral hip displacement on X-ray; it has no role in communication.
added_why_not.Treat hip displacement using antiepilept: Hip displacement is a mechanical, progressive problem needing radiographic surveillance and orthopaedic management; antiseizure drugs do not affect it.
added_why_not.Stop routine examination because GMFCS i: Hip displacement risk rises with GMFCS level and continues through growth; surveillance continues even when motor level is stable.
added_why_not.Wait for complete dislocation before ima: Surveillance aims to detect migration early, while preventive soft-tissue or reconstructive surgery can still avoid painful dislocation.
added_why_not.Cobb scoliosis angle: The Cobb angle measures spinal curvature, not hip displacement.
added_why_not.Tönnis angle as the only CP surveillance: The Tönnis (acetabular) angle describes acetabular dysplasia; CP hip surveillance uses Reimers migration percentage.
added_why_not.Bone age by Greulich–Pyle: Bone age estimates skeletal maturity from a hand X-ray; it does not quantify hip displacement.
added_why_not.Use intrathecal baclofen as mandatory fi: Intrathecal baclofen is for severe generalised spasticity or dystonia; focal dynamic overactivity is treated with targeted botulinum toxin.
added_why_not.Perform irreversible multilevel surgery: Without fixed contracture, dynamic equinus is managed with tone reduction and therapy; surgery is for fixed deformity, usually later.
added_why_not.Use levodopa as sole established treatme: Levodopa is used for dopa-responsive dystonia; it is not an established spasticity treatment.
added_why_not.Escalate only anticholinergic for range: Anticholinergics such as trihexyphenidyl treat dystonia; they cannot restore range lost to fixed contracture.
added_why_not.Treat as chorea without examination: Chorea is an involuntary hyperkinetic movement; loss of range on slow stretch under relaxation is a contracture and needs examination.
added_why_not.Assume all restriction is dynamic spasti: Restriction persisting on slow stretch and under relaxation is fixed contracture, not velocity-dependent spasticity.
added_why_not.Action-specific dystonic posturing only: Dystonia is patterned posturing triggered by action; velocity-dependent catch with clasp-knife release is spasticity.
added_why_not.Constant rigidity independent of movemen: Rigidity is velocity-independent (lead-pipe or cogwheel); resistance that increases with speed and gives way is spasticity.
added_why_not.Pure weakness without reflex change: Weakness alone does not cause increased resistance; velocity-dependent resistance with clasp-knife reflects stretch-reflex hyperexcitability.
added_why_not.Isolated pyramidal weakness: Pyramidal lesions cause weakness and velocity-dependent spasticity, not twisting postures triggered by voluntary movement.
added_why_not.Physiological tremor without posturing: Tremor is a rhythmic oscillation; twisting postures with overflow and fluctuating tone are dystonia.
added_why_not.Cerebellar hypotonia without abnormal mo: Cerebellar lesions cause hypotonia and ataxia, not patterned twisting postures with overflow.
added_why_not.Pure spastic hemiplegia: Hemiplegia gives unilateral weakness and hyperreflexia; dysmetria, intention tremor and a wide-based gait are cerebellar.
added_why_not.Generalized rigidity: Rigidity is velocity-independent increased tone (extrapyramidal); this child has cerebellar signs without increased tone.
added_why_not.Isolated lower motor-neuron paralysis: Lower motor neuron disease gives weakness, wasting and areflexia, not dysmetria and intention tremor.
added_why_not.Spasticity during rapid stretch: Spasticity is resistance to passive stretch, not spontaneous violent flinging of a limb.
added_why_not.Typical essential tremor: Essential tremor is a rhythmic, usually bilateral postural or action tremor, not large-amplitude proximal flinging.
added_why_not.Tics with suppressibility as a defining: Tics are brief, stereotyped and suppressible with a premonitory urge; violent unilateral proximal flinging after a subthalamic/deep lesion is hemiballismus.
added_why_not.Spasticity confined to fast stretch: Spasticity is a tone abnormality found on examination, not spontaneous blinking and jerks with a premonitory urge.
added_why_not.Epileptic myoclonus necessarily with los: Myoclonic seizures are brief jerks often with preserved awareness, and have no premonitory urge or voluntary suppressibility; urge plus suppressibility defines tics.
added_why_not.Athetosis with no urge: Athetosis is slow, continuous writhing, mainly of the hands, without an urge or suppressibility.
added_why_not.Sustained stereotyped torsional dystonia: Dystonia is sustained, patterned twisting; random flowing movements that migrate between body parts are chorea.
added_why_not.Regular oscillatory postural tremor only: Tremor is regular and rhythmic; chorea is irregular and unpredictable.
added_why_not.Atonic weakness: Atonia is loss of tone, not excessive flowing involuntary movement.
added_why_not.Progressive cerebellar ataxia: Ataxia causes incoordination and gait instability, not rhythmic flapping that stops with engagement.
added_why_not.New epileptic spasms are established by: Epileptic spasms are brief axial flexor or extensor contractions, often in clusters on waking, with EEG changes; they are not triggered by excitement or stopped by distraction.
added_why_not.Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia: PKD gives brief dystonic or choreic attacks triggered by sudden movement, usually from later childhood, with preserved awareness.
added_why_not.Treat cough as spasticity exclusively: Coughing with thin liquids and recurrent chest infections indicates aspiration from oropharyngeal dysphagia.
added_why_not.Assume no dysphagia when weight is norma: Normal weight does not exclude unsafe swallowing; silent and overt aspiration occur at any nutritional status.
added_why_not.Increase thin liquids without assessment: Thin liquids are the consistency most often aspirated; a swallow assessment is needed before changing consistency.
added_why_not.Defer communication support until indepe: Communication support should not wait for motor milestones; AAC should start early.
added_why_not.Conclude intellectual disability from ab: Severe dysarthria is a motor speech disorder; comprehension is good, so cognition must not be judged from speech output.
added_why_not.Use muscle relaxant as substitute for sp: Muscle relaxants do not improve communication; augmentative and alternative communication is the intervention.
added_why_not.Assume behavior is purely psychological: In nonverbal children with CP, irritability and sleep disturbance often signal pain — hip, constipation, reflux, dental or fracture.
added_why_not.Ignore symptoms without verbal pain scor: Nonverbal children need observational pain tools (e.g. r-FLACC); absent self-report does not mean absent pain.
added_why_not.Increase tone medication without examini: The cause of discomfort must be found first; raising tone medication may sedate without treating hip pain, constipation or reflux.
added_why_not.Wait until genetic test is normal before: Early intervention should not wait for aetiological tests; genetic testing runs alongside therapy.
added_why_not.Tell family that MRI alone determines li: MRI helps predict topography and risk but does not determine individual functional outcome, which is followed with standardised tools.
added_why_not.Withhold treatment until GMFCS stable at: GMFCS is reasonably stable from about 2–5 years; delaying intervention until adolescence loses the window of neuroplasticity.
added_why_not.Fixed splitting from ASD: ASD causes wide, fixed splitting that does not vary with respiration.
added_why_not.Paradoxical splitting from LBBB: In paradoxical splitting the interval narrows in inspiration and widens in expiration (A2 delayed by LBBB or LV outflow obstruction).
added_why_not.Widely split S2 from pulmonary stenosis: Pulmonary stenosis delays P2, giving a persistently wide split that still varies somewhat, often with a soft P2 and ejection murmur.
added_why_not.PGE1 as sole definitive treatment: PGE1 keeps the duct open but cannot relieve pulmonary venous obstruction and may worsen pulmonary oedema; it is not definitive.
added_why_not.Elective observation until 6 months: Obstructed TAPVC is a neonatal surgical emergency; delay is often fatal.
added_why_not.Balloon aortic valvotomy: Balloon aortic valvotomy treats critical aortic stenosis; it has no role in TAPVC.
added_why_not.Routine annual follow-up: New chest pain, hypotension and pericardial effusion after device closure suggest erosion with tamponade, which is an emergency.
added_why_not.Treat uncomplicated viral pain only: A post-device effusion with hypotension must be treated as device erosion until proven otherwise.
added_why_not.Reassure without imaging: Urgent echocardiography is mandatory to look for tamponade and device erosion.
added_why_not.Apical muscular: Muscular VSDs are common in neonates and often close spontaneously, but perimembranous defects are the most common overall.
added_why_not.Outlet subarterial: Subarterial (doubly committed) VSDs are uncommon in Western series, though more frequent in Asian populations; they are not the most common type.
added_why_not.Inlet: Inlet VSDs are typical of AV septal defects and are relatively uncommon in isolation.
added_why_not.Type B: Krichenko type B is window-like: short, with a narrow aortic end.
added_why_not.Type C: Krichenko type C is tubular, without a constriction.
added_why_not.Type E: Krichenko type E is elongated with a remote constriction, not conical.
added_why_not.Subpulmonary infundibular stenosis: Infundibular stenosis is right ventricular outflow obstruction (as in TOF), not an elongated LV outflow.
added_why_not.Double-chambered right ventricle: DCRV is a muscle band dividing the right ventricle, often with a perimembranous VSD; it does not involve the LVOT.
added_why_not.Restrictive muscular VSD: A small muscular VSD does not produce the elongated, narrowed LV outflow with an unwedged aorta seen in AVSD.
added_why_not.Partial AVSD: Partial AVSD has a primum ASD and two separate AV valve orifices with no ventricular-level shunt.
added_why_not.Complete AVSD: Complete AVSD has a common AV valve with a large, nonrestrictive inlet VSD.
added_why_not.Isolated secundum ASD: A secundum ASD is in the fossa ovalis, with normal AV valves and no inlet VSD.
added_why_not.Balloon mitral valvotomy: Balloon mitral valvotomy treats mitral stenosis, not RV outflow obstruction.
added_why_not.Atrial septostomy as treatment of RVOTO: Septostomy improves atrial mixing (e.g. TGA) but does not increase pulmonary blood flow across an obstructed RVOT.
added_why_not.Pulmonary-vein stenting: Pulmonary-vein stenting treats pulmonary vein stenosis, not TOF RVOT obstruction.
added_why_not.CPS first 48 h; PES after 72 h: The windows are reversed: CPS uses the first 72 h as its transitional framework and PES evaluates persistence after 48 h.
added_why_not.Both use only 24 h: Neither framework uses a single 24-hour window.
added_why_not.Both use only 7 days: Neither framework uses a 7-day boundary for transitional hypoglycaemia.
